extracted.intended_audience: judges, lawyers, examining magistrates, and forensic practitioners assessing witness reliability
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidelines for evaluating the reliability of witness testimony by examining how human sensory perception (vision, hearing, taste, smell, touch) can produce systematic errors or illusions; includes when and how to test senses and what factors to note. Aimed at judicial/forensic assessment of eyewitness and sensory-based testimony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess color-vision normality
rubrics_metrics.description: When color is relevant, determine whether the person has normal color-vision, or the nature and degree of any abnormality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not attempt to resolve philosophical qualia questions; practically test for color-blindness or anomalous perception because objective differences exist that are perceived even by some abnormal eyes. Establish whether the witness's eyes are 'normal' relative to the majority before accepting color-based testimony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify color recognizability at distance with background
rubrics_metrics.description: Single tints may or may not be recognizable at distance depending on tint and background.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use empirical measures (Aubert's angles/table) as a guide: the angle at which colors remain distinguishable varies greatly and depends strongly on whether the background is white or black. Always establish the color seen and the nature of its background before judging such testimony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for different order of color disappearance in dim light
rubrics_metrics.description: Colors fade at different rates as brightness diminishes; red disappears before blue in many cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a witness reports seeing certain colors at dusk/night (e.g., blue coat seen but not red trousers), consider that order-of-fading may make such testimony plausible. Lack of reliable universal order means this factor helps explanation but is not definitive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware peripheral invisibility of red
rubrics_metrics.description: The retina often does not perceive red in the peripheral visual field because red-sensitive receptors are lacking there.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a witness saw a red object askance (not fixated), their color report is unreliable; simple experiments can demonstrate this (drag a red object across vision).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider color-induced size/shape illusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Colors influence apparent size and length: less refractable colors (red, orange, yellow, purple) may appear slightly larger; blue/green may appear smaller.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When witnesses judge size/length, note the object's color—Quantz's percentages (0.2–3.6% larger or 0.2–2.2% smaller) indicate systematic bias useful in assessing small size/length discrepancies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize hue changes through small apertures
rubrics_metrics.description: Viewing colors through small openings or holes can alter perceived nuances and even desaturate green.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If witness viewed an object through a small gap, their color description may be distorted; determine viewing aperture conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain 'sparkle' and glint illusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Sparkle is perceived when one point is bright and brightness drops sharply nearby; such localized highlights can generate false impressions of shining weapons or coins.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under certain illumination or distance, dull objects may appear to 'sparkle' and be misreported as weapons or coins. Investigate lighting conditions and expect false-positive sightings where glints could occur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for blind spot size and fixation effects
rubrics_metrics.description: The physiological blind spot enlarges with distance and is largely unnoticed because vision 'fills in' the void; fixation and interest affect whether missing parts are perceived.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume the textbook small blind spot is inconsequential; at distance it can cover large areas (e.g., human face). Consider whether the witness was fixating elsewhere, whether both eyes were used, and whether interest/attention could have caused omission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider askance observations and blind-spot explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: Objects seen askance may be missed due to blind spots or peripheral limitations; such explanations are conceivable even if rare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although practical cases may be uncommon, keep blind-spot effects in mind when a witness reports not seeing something that might have been in their peripheral field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect witnesses to reproduce meaning, not exact words
rubrics_metrics.description: Witnesses typically remember the sense or meaning of spoken words rather than verbatim wording; they tend to substitute words that fit the meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not expect literal recall without special training; uneducated witnesses especially may recall only meaning. In slander/insult cases, expect paraphrase or category-based substitution of epithets rather than exact lexical recall.

rubrics_metrics.name: Never rely solely on informal vocal tests for hearing ability
rubrics_metrics.description: Determining a person's hearing power requires expert examination under conditions matching the original situation; casual vocal tests are insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For important cases, engage an expert audiologist and, if possible, recreate original place, people, and conditions to approximate what was heard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish auditory detection from auditory discrimination
rubrics_metrics.description: Hearing ability includes not just whether tones/noises are detected but whether a person can isolate and retain a single tone among many.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tests must probe discrimination (ability to pick a tone out of others) because this varies by individual, time, place, and voice; uncontrolled simple tests will misestimate capability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of selective auditory attention and variability
rubrics_metrics.description: Individuals can selectively attend to different simultaneous sounds on different occasions; performance can change day-to-day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A single observation of hearing (or failure to) is not definitive. Where precise auditory testimony matters, perform repeated and controlled examinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize high/low tone perception differences
rubrics_metrics.description: Some people fail to hear high tones (e.g., cricket chirps) despite otherwise acute hearing; others perceive low tones as rolls/roars rather than individual tones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the frequency content of the sound involved when evaluating testimony about specific noises; an ordinary 'normal' hearing label may mask such frequency-specific deficits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat directional judgments of sound as unreliable
rubrics_metrics.description: Humans commonly misjudge sound direction (front vs back confusions; height errors); lateral (right/left) distinctions are usually better.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When direction of sound is material, seek evidence of binaural hearing and conduct experiments; ask physician to check whether the witness hears equally with both ears, as unilateral hearing degrades directional ability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow for sound conduction through solids and structures
rubrics_metrics.description: Sound can travel strikingly well through compact bodies (ground, walls, built-in baths), enabling hearing at distances or through structures where airborne hearing would fail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a witness reports hearing horse trotting or knocks by placing ear to ground or wall, do not dismiss; attempt to approximate the physical conduction path to evaluate plausibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider underwater and structure-mediated hearing differences
rubrics_metrics.description: When ears are submerged, airborne sounds are largely inaudible while noises conducted by solid structures (walls, bath) can be clear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In drowning, eavesdropping, or bathroom incidents, note whether the ear was submerged and whether sound conduction via structures could explain testimony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for deafness patterns, lip-reading, age, occupation, and sex effects on hearing
rubrics_metrics.description: Deafness typically begins with high tones and progresses; deaf persons may compensate by lip-reading; hearing declines with age and noisy occupations harm hearing; sex differences are reported but mixed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take a full history of age, occupation (noisy trades), tobacco use, and any lip-reading practice. Use population data (e.g., reduced conversational understanding over certain distances in >50s) to weight testimony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat taste testimony cautiously and involve medical expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: Taste is rarely legally important except in poisoning; taste descriptions use many subjective descriptors and are influenced by age, habit, health, and intelligence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where taste is material, call a physician, test systematically, and note whether the taste was perceived at tongue-tip or root (Longet's distinctions). Beware idiosyncratic descriptors and variable usage of terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use olfactory associations as investigative leads
rubrics_metrics.description: Smell has powerful associative memory and can awaken remote, vivid recollections that witnesses may initially call 'accidental'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use careful questioning to surface olfactory-linked memories. Note that practice dulls smell (butchers, perfumers), occupation/habits (smoking) affect acuity, and individual preferences/conditions (hunger, migraine) alter valence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ask whether the witness actually touched an object when citing tactile details
rubrics_metrics.description: Tactile reports about texture, smoothness, fineness, etc., are only reliable if the witness physically tested the object (e.g., with fingertips).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifically ask whether and how the object was touched. Blind and trained individuals can have exceptional tactile acuity; consider whether the witness relies on touch or merely on memory or inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider training, muscular use, sex, and drugs on touch sensitivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Touch sensitivity is improved by practice and muscle training, tends to be finer in women, and is altered by injections/medications (morphine, cannabinum tannicum, alcohol).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When touch-sense testimony matters, obtain relevant history of training, occupation, sex, and recent drug use or medical treatment that could alter sensitivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Note variability and limits in temperature perception
rubrics_metrics.description: Temperature differences as small as 0.2 degrees can be perceived at lips and fingertips, but absolute temperature estimates vary (mean error often ~4 degrees); familiarity with a specific environment improves accuracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept narrow-range temperature judgments when the witness is accustomed to that condition (e.g., habitual room temperature), but treat absolute numeric temperature assertions skeptically unless conditions are controlled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect localization errors and skin transpositions after vigorous movement
rubrics_metrics.description: When skin is pulled or body parts moved (twists, holds), the mapping of stimulation to body location can be displaced, making precise localization of blows/wounds difficult.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate body position and movements during the event; consider that a blow felt in one place may have been applied to another area because of skin shifts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand temporal delay and qualitative nature of pain perception
rubrics_metrics.description: There can be a measurable delay between stimulus and reported pain (historically reported ~1/30 to 1/3 second); victims often describe stabs as pushes and may not feel blade cold, while perpetrators report clearer sensation of entry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate reports from the wounded and the wounder: wounded persons often sense a hard push rather than a sharp stab and may misattribute sensations. Helplines: explain these perceptual facts to witnesses to elicit more accurate accounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware wetness and blood-feel confusions
rubrics_metrics.description: The sensation of wetness is a compound of coldness and movement; smooth cold metal can be mistaken for blood and vice versa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When witnesses report feeling blood or wetness, probe whether they tested temperature, texture, or movement; consider plausible confusions in chaotic situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remember summation: repetition intensifies touch sensations
rubrics_metrics.description: Repetition or summation of tactile stimuli increases intensity and clarity of the sensation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take into account whether repeated contact occurred (which would intensify perception) or whether isolated brief contacts were reported; this affects the plausibility and character of tactile testimony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for individual and contextual modifiers across senses
rubrics_metrics.description: Across all senses, age, sex, education, occupation, nervousness, practice/habituation, and recent medication or intoxication significantly alter perception and reportability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gather full personal, occupational, medical, and situational context (lighting, distance, fixation, binaural hearing, viewing aperture, etc.) and whenever necessary obtain expert physiological or medical examinations to calibrate witness reliability.
